chapters.title: A long way home.
chapters.quote: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy.
chapters.source: Homer · The Odyssey, Book I · trans. Samuel Butler
chapters.body: The invocation begins with a traveller and a perilous return. Our sheet holds an extract from the opening, with the translator named. Read it slowly; the wider story remains there to be entered.
chapters.image_alt: An imagined Mediterranean shore at dawn.

chapters.title: Words to receive with care.
chapters.quote: Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.
chapters.source: Jesus of Nazareth · Matthew 5:7 · Authorized Version
chapters.body: The Beatitudes belong to the opening of the Sermon on the Mount. This verse is one of the blessings; the broadside carries Matthew 5:3–12 together, with verse numbers beside the words.
chapters.image_alt: An imagined olive hillside overlooking a lake.

chapters.title: The question remains.
chapters.quote: For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?
chapters.source: Jesus of Nazareth · Matthew 16:26 · Authorized Version
chapters.body: Two questions, kept together. The passage asks about the soul and the cost of worldly gain. Its weight belongs to the Gospel itself; the sheet gives it a place to be read and considered.
chapters.image_alt: An open stone doorway leading to a sunlit, dry hillside path.

chapters.title: A prayer on the page.
chapters.quote: Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.
chapters.source: Augustine · Confessions, Book I · trans. E. B. Pusey
chapters.body: Augustine addresses God in the opening of the Confessions. The restless heart is held within that prayer. We preserve that address, and name the translation beneath the passage.
chapters.image_alt: A secluded stone courtyard with a cypress and an empty bench.

chapters.title: At the edge of the wood.
chapters.quote:
Midway upon the journey of our life
I found myself within a forest dark,
For the straightforward pathway had been lost.
chapters.source: Dante · Inferno, Canto I, lines 1–3 · trans. H. W. Longfellow
chapters.body: The Divine Comedy opens with a lost path. These three lines mark the beginning of a much larger journey. The sheet keeps Longfellow’s line breaks, and gives the source its own line.
chapters.image_alt: An imagined woodland path in the morning light.

narration: Some words ask us to slow down. To read again. To make room.
Homer opens with a traveller, far from home. An old story, still asking for our attention.
In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus teaches: Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.
Elsewhere in Matthew, a question weighs the whole world against the soul.
Augustine brings his restless heart to God. A prayer, still held on the page.
Dante begins in a dark wood, with the way ahead lost.
Poetry. Scripture. Prayer. Art. Distinct works, each with its own source.
From our press in Austin, words to live with. Explore the Western Canon at Thomas Broadside Company.
